v.why: Removing a redundant conv on the input-output edge costs little, while removing a skip there (the alternative parents) destroys the residual path and hurts.
Adding a residual connection where none existed improves trainability of the stacked network more than swapping it in for an existing op.
Replacing the weakest op (parameter-free pooling) on the node2-to-output edge with a 3x3 conv gives a larger gain than replacing a skip or another conv.
When edge 0 is none, node 1 is dead, so adding a conv reactivates the paths through edges 2 and 4 and adds depth and capacity.
Deleting a conv on the edge into the output removes real learned capacity, whereas deleting a skip or pool there is often neutral or helpful.
Removing a conv on edge 1 is mild because node 2 still gets conv input via node 1, but removing a skip on edge 1 cuts a short gradient path and hurts more.
Swapping a 3x3 conv for pooling loses capacity, whereas swapping none or skip for pooling at worst adds a cheap smoothing path.
Replacing the input-output skip with a 1x1 conv eliminates the residual identity path that top NB201 cells rely on.
When edge 5 is none, node 2 does not reach the output, so removing edge 1 has roughly zero effect instead of its usual mildly negative effect.
Turning a lossy pooling shortcut into a true identity residual helps more than replacing a conv that already carries useful features.

raw:
Several measurements conflict with each other, and some deltas are implausibly large. So I based these hypotheses on NAS-Bench-201's known structure as well as the data:

- A skip connection on edge 3 (0→3) acts as a residual and matters a lot.
- `nor_conv_3x3` is generally the strongest operation and `avg_pool_3x3` generally the weakest.
- When edge 5 is `none`, node 2 has no effect on the output, so edits on edge 1 do nothing.
